title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit that applied conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap; provenance heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy to a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample. Crucially, the archived execution used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (task_manifest entries with source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") and shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) and execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256: b7c08599e3f96d8d5605a18f8f973e0707d7224327eeed7bde78c0d34cb83e55). Because baseline and guarded episodes reused the same shared generation per item (model_calls_used = 150), the primary confirmatory estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) was rendered degenerate/untestable for detecting generation‑level contamination in this run. Artifact‑verified results: no preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags (analysis/contamination_summary.csv; SHA‑256: 389227f0d1e81239c7498abd4944a04c59c92c5fa042b990e332796cd61c3222), baseline = 150/150 passes, guarded = 150/150 passes, paired difference = 0.0 pp (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0). We provide an explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation (preregistration SHA‑256: 9a5e11c5b2b1c14c2a4a874a7ad0b9f215f8477a7becf4eb6dd1c0ff6a00ae7a), diagnose why the run is uninformative for public‑benchmark leakage, and give artifact‑anchored recommendations to increase audit sensitivity.

sections.introduction:
Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) are being applied to NetOps tasks such as intent‑to‑configuration translation and automated configuration repair. Benchmarks and system evaluations drive operational confidence, but measurement validity is threatened if benchmark items or templated prompts appear in model training data (contamination) or if benchmarks emphasize low‑complexity templated items (construct invalidity). Surveys and recent meta‑analyses therefore recommend contamination detectors (lexical fingerprinting, n‑gram overlap) and provenance tracing plus verify‑driven oracles to bound inflated reliability claims.

Research question and contribution. We preregistered an audit (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) to test: under conservative deterministic contamination detectors and a preregistered guarded exclusion policy, how many high‑confidence flags arise in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample, and how much does applying those controls change a hosted LLM's validator pass rate? We report: (1) a completed preregistered experiment with frozen estimands and rules (preregistration SHA‑256: 9a5e11c5b2b1c14c2a4a874a7ad0b9f215f8477a7becf4eb6dd1c0ff6a00ae7a); (2) artifact‑verified outcomes on Npairs = 150 (analysis artifacts: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256: c2ba9cdb5d0938eae910129ba511eadf309319e6e05b36d9e3b4860032deb80e); and (3) an explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation that documents why the primary inferential test was degenerate in this execution and prescribes concrete, artifact‑anchored corrective steps for future audits.

Scope and bounded claims. The experiment tested the operational behavior of the preregistered detector suite and guarded policy under the executed sampling and generation semantics. It did not sample the public OpenAlex benchmark items named in the preregistration's benchmark_scope (OpenAlex identifiers: W7157506260, W4404602270, W4404534210, W7166900660). The executed sample instead used deterministic synthetic items (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256: b7c08599e3f96d8d5605a18f8f973e0707d7224327eeed7bde78c0d34cb83e55). Because these execution facts are recorded in the archive, the observed zero‑flag, zero‑difference outcome applies only to this synthetic, shared‑generation regime and not to web‑sourced benchmarks.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑for‑NetOps and validator integrations. Prior system and benchmark studies show that LLMs can map intent to configuration artifacts and that integrating formal verifiers or iterative validate–repair loops improves repair reliability (e.g., recent benchmarks and agentic repair systems). Formal network verification tools such as Header Space Analysis and localized subspecification methods provide practical oracles for reachability and policy checks and are commonly used in generate–validate pipelines.

Evaluation validity and contamination. Methodological critiques and surveys identify contamination and templating as systematic evaluation threats and recommend deterministic fingerprinting, fuzzy n‑gram overlap, and provenance metadata reporting. Our work implements a conservative subset of these defenses within a preregistered confirmatory design and focuses on the preregistration→execution reconciliation required when archived execution semantics differ from preregistered sampling assumptions.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen analysis. The preregistration (study_id above; preregistration SHA‑256: 9a5e11c5b2b1c14c2a4a874a7ad0b9f215f8477a7becf4eb6dd1c0ff6a00ae7a) froze: the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), contamination detectors and thresholds (exact normalized token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap with high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80), exclusion/replacement rules (exclude high‑confidence flags and deterministically replace with retemplated items meeting cosine ≥ 0.85), sampling plan (task_count = 150), and the analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). The preregistration's benchmark_scope listed four public OpenAlex records (W7157506260, W4404602270, W4404534210, W7166900660) as candidate data sources.

Sampling and generation semantics. To ensure reproducibility the preregistration allowed deterministic synthetic generation. The executed pipeline used deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and produced tasks whose manifest entries carry source_identifier values beginning "synthetic-netops:" (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256: b7c08599e3f96d8d5605a18f8f973e0707d7224327eeed7bde78c0d34cb83e55). The executed model configuration declared gpt-5-mini and independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics) in execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). Under this choice the pipeline made one model generation per item and reused that candidate for both baseline and guarded episodes unless an exclusion/replacement occurred, reducing model_calls_used to 150 (execution manifest). This execution fact mechanically collapses baseline vs guarded discordance in the absence of flagged exclusions.

Contamination detectors, persistence policy, and artifacts. The preregistered detector suite implemented: (1) exact normalized token equality, (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap with high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80, and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics. The detector workflow was implemented to persist detailed per‑item fuzzy overlap tables only when threshold crossings or replacements occurred; that persistence policy is documented in the archived transformation manifest (execution/transformation_manifest.json; path present in the bundle). In this execution no high‑confidence flags occurred and therefore no global per‑item overlap table artifact was created. The absence of flags is evidenced by analysis/contamination_summary.csv (SHA‑256: 389227f0d1e81239c7498abd4944a04c59c92c5fa042b990e332796cd61c3222), which contains no flagged rows. This implementation choice reduced stored artifacts in the no‑flag case but also removed the possibility of reporting per‑item overlap distributions post‑hoc.

Validator and scoring. The deterministic oracle deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0) parsed candidate configurations, simulated their application to explicit device/state models, and checked required_final_state and workflow constraints (full_intent_constraint_validation). The validator emitted binary pass/fail outcomes and per‑episode traces (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes). These traces were archived for each episode and form the empirical basis for outcomes (execution/scoring/*.json; representative examples archived in execution/scoring/; see artifact examples).

Analysis executor and inferential plan. The preregistered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor computed the paired contingency table (n11,n10,n01,n00), performed an exact McNemar two‑sided test, and estimated a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). The primary confirmatory test was the single prespecified paired test (H2); secondary prespecified analyses included fuzzy‑threshold sensitivity and subgroup analyses. The preregistration specified replacement rules and replacement generation seeds to preserve determinism if exclusions occurred.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation. Execution completed planned_episode_count = 300 episodes (150 item pairs) with completed_episode_count = 300 and failed_episode_count = 0. Because independent_condition_generation = false and no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, the pipeline used model_calls_used = 150 (one shared generation per item) rather than two separate generations per condition; provider call accounting is recorded in the deterministic_reconciliation artifact (SHA‑256: 57c70942a9ffa93f7a2cb0c87c8996fcf12d516066a3ce6b5dcbb33add40b8b8). The analysis/condition_summary.csv shows baseline successes = 150/150 and guarded successes = 150/150 (analysis/condition_summary.csv; SHA‑256: 9d3de16521f01d53c002b69512a6edc0253a8953e413faeed5d1c0feb3e6d4f9).

Contamination detectors: absence of preregistered high‑confidence flags. The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence flags for the executed sample. The analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty of flagged rows (SHA‑256 above). Because detector persistence was conditional on threshold crossings, the archive lacks a global per‑item overlap table for this execution; this absence is an explicit artifact of the detector persistence policy (execution/transformation_manifest.json — path present in bundle) and is evidenced by the empty contamination_summary.csv (SHA‑256 above).

Primary estimand and inferential outcome (artifact‑verified degeneracy). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256: c2ba9cdb5d0938eae910129ba511eadf309319e6e05b36d9e3b4860032deb80e). The computed paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0 percentage points; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. These numbers are artifact‑grounded and correct. But because baseline and guarded outputs were identical by construction absent replacements (shared generation), the primary estimand was rendered untestable for generation‑level contamination in this execution: the null result is a degeneracy produced by execution semantics rather than persuasive evidence of absence of contamination in external benchmarks.

Representative episode diagnostic. Representative archived episodes (e.g., pair‑000001; task‑000001) show identical normalized response and reference answer strings and validator parsed_command_count = required_command_count (see execution/scoring/task‑000001‑baseline.json; raw response and validator_trace hashes recorded in the bundle). These exemplars illustrate validator behavior and confirm that the deterministic validator accepted the generated configurations under the specified scoring rule.
sections.discussion:
Why the run was uninformative for public‑benchmark leakage. Two recorded execution facts explain the degenerate concordance (n11 = 150): (1) the confirmatory sample was drawn from deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 with source_identifier values prefixed "synthetic-netops:" (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256: b7c08599...), so sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic tasks rather than the preregistered public OpenAlex datasets; and (2) the pipeline executed with shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) declared in execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256: a40e96e2...), causing one model generation per item to be reused for both baseline and guarded episodes in the absence of exclusions. Both artifacts are archived and substantiate the preregistration→execution divergence.

Detector persistence policy and missing overlap summaries. The detector workflow persisted per‑item overlap scores only upon threshold crossings or replacement events; this conditional persistence behavior is documented in the transformation manifest (execution/transformation_manifest.json — path present in bundle) and explains why no per‑item overlap table exists for this run. The empty contamination_summary.csv (SHA‑256: 389227f0...) confirms no high‑confidence flags were produced. Because the archive lacks a full per‑item overlap distribution for this execution, readers cannot reconstruct how close items were to the preregistered fuzzy thresholds; we therefore recommend persisting all per‑item overlap scores in future audits regardless of threshold crossings.

Design changes to increase audit sensitivity (artifact‑anchored). The archived artifacts support concrete corrective steps: (a) sample provenance‑rich public items (use the preregistration benchmark_scope OpenAlex IDs) rather than synthetic items; (b) set independent_condition_generation = true to force independent generations per condition (recordable in execution/model_configuration.json) and thus enable observation of discordant pairs; (c) persist all per‑item fuzzy overlap scores into analysis/contamination_scores.csv to permit sensitivity curves; (d) expand to multiple model instances/seeds (increase model_calls_used) to raise power; and (e) include paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication for borderline cases. Each recommendation follows directly from gaps visible in the archived artifacts: model_calls_used = 150 (execution manifest), an empty contamination_summary.csv (analysis artifact), and absence of a per‑item overlap table.

Operational implications and caution. The artifact‑verified validator traces confirm that the deterministic oracle can certify functional constraints on generated configurations; however, the audit's synthetic sampling and sharedgeneration semantics preclude extrapolation to web‑sourced benchmarks. For operational risk assessment, auditors should combine provenance‑rich sampling, cross‑model replication, independent generation per condition, and human adjudication to obtain evidence applicable to production corpora.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifact‑anchored audit of conservative contamination detectors in an LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluation pipeline. Artifact evidence shows zero preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator pass rates in the executed 150‑pair synthetic sample. Crucially, the primary confirmatory estimand was rendered untestable in this run because baseline and guarded outputs were identical by construction under shared_initial_candidate semantics (execution/model_configuration.json; SHA‑256: a40e96e2...). We provide a compact preregistration→execution reconciliation (preregistration SHA‑256: 9a5e11c5...) and recommend implementable artifact‑anchored changes—public sampling, independent generation, per‑item overlap persistence, and multi‑model replication—to make future contamination audits sensitive to web‑sourced leakage. All artifacts cited above are archived in the execution bundle and substantiate the claims made here.

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require richer provenance or human adjudication.

Passing deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
